claims.text: The WTaTiVZr alloy is nearly single-phase with a BCC or near-BCC structure.
The WTaTiVZr alloy has a refined, possibly nanocrystalline grain structure.
The refined alloy contains a high density of high-angle grain boundaries.
Chemical disorder in equimolar WTaTiVZr produces significant local lattice distortions.
WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain and toughness than commercially pure tungsten.
Local lattice distortions lower the effective barrier to dislocation motion in WTaTiVZr.
Refined grain boundaries promote grain-boundary-mediated deformation at high temperature.
The lattice distortions and refined grain structure encourage dynamic recovery in WTaTiVZr at high temperature.
Pure tungsten has high Peierls barriers that favor dislocation pile-up and cleavage.
Commercially pure tungsten undergoes minimal plastic deformation and brittle failure under the specified high-temperature loading.
The proposed mechanism shifts deformation from pile-up and cleavage to a more homogeneous grain-boundary-mediated process.
At temperatures of about 800 °C or higher, thermal activation is sufficient to enable dynamic recovery and grain-boundary processes.
Under identical loading, WTaTiVZr should exhibit evidence of grain-boundary sliding, dynamic recovery, uniform deformation, and ductile fracture.
The comparison should use WTaTiVZr and pure-tungsten specimens with comparable dimensions and surface finishes, tested at the same temperature and strain rate in an inert atmosphere.
The hypothesis is intended to apply only when extrinsic defects such as porosity and oxidation have been eliminated.
Residual secondary phases and oxidation may contribute to the observed high-temperature behavior, but their contributions are not quantified.
Failure to observe a statistically significant ductility and toughness increase, or failure to observe grain-boundary-mediated deformation and dynamic recovery, would falsify the hypothesis.
